lessons.title: Expenses Overview and the Expense Lifecycle

slots.practicalActivity: Using Castellan Supply Co. (the course's own 1,400-employee worked example), write the six-stage expense lifecycle from memory -- Incur, Capture, Submit, Audit and Approve, Account, Reimburse -- and for each stage name which role (employee, approver, expense auditor, AP staff, or the Fusion consultant) is primarily involved. Then explain in 2-3 sentences why Expenses is correctly described as a 'feeder' to Payables rather than a standalone payment system.
slots.deliverable: A 6-stage expense-lifecycle-to-role mapping for Castellan Supply Co., plus a written explanation of why Expenses feeds Payables rather than paying directly.

slots.practicalActivity: Design an expense template for Castellan Supply Co.'s traveling sales reps with at least 5 expense types (for example Airfare, Hotel, Business Meal, Ground Transportation, Client Entertainment). For each type, set a policy limit and mark whether it is a hard limit (blocks submission) or a soft limit (allows submission but flags a policy violation). Then write one sentence explaining why a company would deliberately choose a soft limit over a hard limit for a specific expense type.
slots.deliverable: A 5-type expense template for Castellan sales reps with hard/soft limits marked, plus a written justification for one soft-limit choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a sample Castellan expense report for a 3-day client trip with at least 4 expense lines (airfare, hotel, two business meals), then itemize the hotel line into room, tax, and one incidental charge the way the lesson describes breaking a single folio into separate itemized amounts. Attach a placeholder receipt reference to each line and note which lines, if any, could legitimately go without one under Castellan's policy.
slots.deliverable: A 4-line sample expense report for a 3-day trip with the hotel folio itemized into at least 3 components, and receipt requirements noted per line.

slots.practicalActivity: Calculate a mileage reimbursement for a 38-mile round trip at Castellan's $0.67/mile standard rate, then build a 4-day Chicago per diem claim at a $74/day full rate, applying the travel-day 75% rate on day 1 and a breakfast deduction on day 4 the way the lesson works the example. Separately, work the cash-advance math for Jordan Reyes: a $600 advance applied against a $410 expense report, and explain how the resulting $190 owed back to Castellan actually gets collected.
slots.deliverable: A worked mileage calculation, a 4-day per-diem claim with travel-day and meal-deduction adjustments, and a worked cash-advance-shortfall calculation with its collection method explained.

slots.practicalActivity: Design Castellan's corporate card program in three pieces: name the card issuer and which business units use it, write a corporate card usage policy threshold for one expense type (for example, client meals under $50 may go on cash, at/above must use the card), and map 3 merchant category codes to Castellan expense types. Then write a worked comparison showing, for the same $200 hotel charge, who Payables actually pays under an individual-liability card versus a company-liability card.
slots.deliverable: A 3-part corporate card program design for Castellan plus a worked individual-liability-vs-company-liability payment comparison for a $200 hotel charge.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Submitting Expenses: build one continuous Castellan expense report for a single business trip that combines every submission method from this chapter -- a manually entered itemized hotel folio, a mileage claim, a per diem day, an applied cash advance, and at least one corporate card transaction pulled from the unassigned-transactions queue -- and calculate the final net reimbursement amount.
slots.deliverable: One continuous written expense report combining itemized receipts, mileage, per diem, a cash advance, and a card transaction, with a calculated final net reimbursement.

slots.practicalActivity: Recreate the lesson's Dana Oyelaran scenario: a $460/night hotel charge against a 'High-value hotel' audit rule ($400/night threshold, Complete audit action) plus two missing-receipt declarations triggering a separate employee-level rule. Write the audit list rule criteria and action for both rules, then explain, in writing, what the expense auditor reviews and clears before the report moves to the separate manager-approval step, and why audit rules and manager approval are deliberately two different checks.
slots.deliverable: Two written audit list rule specifications (criteria + action) for the Dana Oyelaran scenario, plus an explanation distinguishing the auditor's review from manager approval.

slots.practicalActivity: Trace how Dana Oyelaran's now-approved report (from the previous slot) becomes an actual Payables payment: name what Payables creates from the approved report and who gets paid, given it included both personal-card and company-liability-card lines. Then write a separate scenario where a different report gets rejected by the audit rule instead -- what the employee has to do to correct it, and whether it keeps its original submission date or resets when resubmitted.
slots.deliverable: A written reimbursement-payment trace for the approved Dana Oyelaran report, plus a correction-and-resubmission walkthrough for a rejected report.

lessons.title: Expenses to Payables to General Ledger

slots.practicalActivity: Write the accounting distribution for a $440 approved Castellan expense report with a $600 cash advance applied (recall the Jordan Reyes example): name the debit and credit accounts for the expense lines, the advance clearing account, and the net payable to the employee. Then trace the full path that accounting entry takes from Expenses, through the Payables invoice it generates, to the journal that ultimately posts in the General Ledger.
slots.deliverable: A worked accounting-distribution table for the $440 net reimbursement with applied advance, plus a written Expenses-to-Payables-to-GL trace.

slots.practicalActivity: Name which Expenses report a Castellan finance manager would pull to answer 'how much did Client Entertainment spend cost us by region last quarter,' and sketch what its rows and columns would show. Then, using the course's own troubleshooting-practice lesson as your model, pick 3 realistic Expenses problems (a card transaction that never gets attached to a report, a report stuck in audit, a reimbursement that doesn't match the approved amount) and write a root-cause-and-fix script for each.
slots.deliverable: A named/sketched Client-Entertainment-by-region analysis report plus a 3-problem Expenses troubleshooting script.

lessons.title: Designing Expense Policy for a Real Company

slots.practicalActivity: Recreate the lesson's Harrowgate Freight Logistics discovery exercise: a 600-employee trucking company with 40 traveling regional sales reps, no formal policy history, and two named pain points (fuel-card misuse and unsubstantiated client meals). Write the 4 discovery questions you'd ask the controller, then design Harrowgate's policy framework -- a travel template with hotel/meal caps, a corporate card decision for the 40 reps, and 2 targeted audit rules aimed specifically at the named pain points rather than spread evenly across all spend categories.
slots.deliverable: A 4-question discovery list plus a complete Harrowgate Freight Logistics policy framework (template caps, card decision, and 2 targeted audit rules).

slots.practicalActivity: Course capstone lab: recreate Castellan US Operations' monthly three-way reconciliation -- a $184,620.00 issuer statement total, $184,620.00 received in the transaction feed, and only $179,310.00 attached to approved reports -- identify the $5,310.00 gap, and write the step-by-step monthly reconciliation routine (pull the report, find aged-unassigned transactions, cross-reference the audit list, escalate with a deadline) you'd run to close it. Then close the course by writing one paragraph connecting setup, submission, audit/approval, accounting, and this reconciliation into a single end-to-end Expenses story for a new client.
slots.deliverable: A worked three-way reconciliation identifying the $5,310.00 gap with a written closing routine, plus a one-paragraph end-to-end Expenses lifecycle summary.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can configure Oracle Fusion Expenses end to end -- templates, policies, mileage/per diem, cash advances, and corporate card programs -- and run the audit, approval, Payables reimbursement, accounting, and corporate-card-reconciliation processes a Fusion Financials consultant would own for a real client's expense program.
